definition: **Workflows** run LLMs and tools through predefined code paths. **Agents** let the LLM dynamically direct its own process and tool use.
whyItMatters: Workflows give predictability for well-defined tasks; agents give flexibility at the cost of latency and spend. Start with the simplest solution.
example: A fixed translate → check → format pipeline is a workflow; an assistant that decides which files to edit is an agent.

definition: A rule that ends an agent loop even if the task isn't finished, such as a maximum number of iterations.
whyItMatters: Agent tasks often end on completion, but Anthropic's guidance says it's common to add stopping conditions to maintain control.
example: Stop the loop and report back after 20 tool calls.

definition: A multi-agent design: a lead agent plans the work, spawns subagents that explore in parallel with their own context windows, then synthesizes their findings.
whyItMatters: Anthropic's Research system uses this orchestrator-worker design. It excels at breadth-first queries that pursue several independent directions at once.
example: Finding all board members of S&P 500 IT companies by decomposing it into subagent tasks.

source.title: How we built our multi-agent research system

definition: In Anthropic's data, agents typically use about **4×** more tokens than chat interactions, and multi-agent systems about **15×** more.
whyItMatters: For economic viability, multi-agent systems need tasks whose value is high enough to pay for the increased performance.

source.title: How we built our multi-agent research system

definition: What a lead agent gives each subagent: an objective, an output format, guidance on the tools and sources to use, and clear task boundaries.
whyItMatters: Without detailed task descriptions, subagents duplicate work, leave gaps or fail to find necessary information.
example: Not just "research the semiconductor shortage", but a scoped objective, sources and output format.

source.title: How we built our multi-agent research system

definition: The agent regularly writes notes to memory outside its context window; the notes are pulled back into context at later times.
whyItMatters: It gives persistent memory with minimal overhead, and Anthropic says it excels for iterative development with clear milestones.
example: A custom agent maintaining a `NOTES.md` file to track progress across a complex task.

source.title: Effective context engineering for AI agents

definition: The first session of a long-running harness: it sets up an `init.sh` script, a `claude-progress.txt` log and an initial git commit.
whyItMatters: Each later session starts with a fresh context window, so it reads the progress file and git history to quickly understand the state of work.
example: Session 1 writes the feature list and init.sh; later sessions each work on one feature, then commit.

definition: A JSON file of end-to-end feature requirements, all initially marked failing, that coding agents update only by changing each feature's `passes` field.
whyItMatters: It stops agents declaring the project done too early. JSON is used because the model is less likely to inappropriately change it than Markdown.

definition: Anthropic's advice: find the simplest solution possible and increase complexity only when needed, which might mean not building an agentic system at all.
whyItMatters: Agentic systems often trade latency and cost for better task performance. For many apps, optimizing single LLM calls with retrieval and examples is usually enough.

definition: A Python and TypeScript library giving you the same tools, agent loop and context management that power Claude Code, in a process you operate.
whyItMatters: Choose it over the Client SDK when you want built-in tools, permissions, sessions and hooks instead of writing the tool loop yourself.
example: Embed an agent that finds and fixes bugs in existing code inside your own app.

definition: Agent SDK caps on tool-use turns and on spend. Hitting one ends the loop with an `error_max_turns` or `error_max_budget_usd` result.
whyItMatters: Both default to no limit, so open-ended prompts can run long. Setting a budget is a good default for production agents.
example: `max_turns=30` to prevent runaway sessions; if hit, resume the session with a higher limit.

definition: `allowedTools` auto-approves the listed tools; `disallowedTools` blocks them, even in bypassPermissions mode. Unlisted tools stay available.
whyItMatters: Allowing is not restricting: `allowed_tools` does not constrain `bypassPermissions`. To block a tool there, use `disallowed_tools`.
example: `disallowed_tools=["Bash"]` removes Bash from the request, so Claude cannot attempt it.

definition: An Agent SDK hook callback that fires before a tool executes and can allow, deny or modify the call, for example by returning a deny decision.
whyItMatters: Use it to block dangerous operations before they execute, such as writes to `.env` files. If any hook returns deny, the operation is blocked.
example: A `"Write|Edit"` matcher makes the callback fire only for file-writing tools.

source.title: Intercept and control agent behavior with hooks

definition: Your own function Claude can call: a name, description, input schema and handler, wrapped in an in-process MCP server with `createSdkMcpServer`.
whyItMatters: Tools are named `mcp__{server_name}__{tool_name}`. Returning `isError: true` lets you compose the error message Claude reads.
example: A `get_temperature` tool registered on a `weather` server.

definition: A non-fork subagent starts fresh: its own system prompt plus the Agent tool's prompt, without the parent's history. Only its final message returns.
whyItMatters: The Agent tool's prompt string is the only content passed from parent to subagent, so include file paths, errors and decisions in it.
example: A doc-reviewer subagent limited to Read and Grep can analyze files but never modify them.

definition: A pre-built, configurable agent harness that runs in managed infrastructure, built around four concepts: agent, environment, session and events.
whyItMatters: Best for long-running tasks and asynchronous work. The Messages API is best for custom agent loops and fine-grained control.
example: Create an agent once, then start sessions that reference it by ID.

definition: A workflow that splits a task into a sequence of steps, each LLM call processing the previous output, with optional programmatic checks (gates) between steps.
whyItMatters: Ideal when a task decomposes cleanly into fixed subtasks. It trades latency for higher accuracy by making each LLM call an easier task.
example: Write an outline, check it meets criteria, then write the document from the outline.

definition: A workflow that classifies an input and directs it to a specialized follow-up task, such as a different prompt, tool set or model.
whyItMatters: Use it when distinct categories are better handled separately; without it, optimizing for one kind of input can hurt performance on others.
example: Send easy, common questions to a smaller, cost-efficient model and hard ones to a more capable one.

definition: LLMs work on a task simultaneously and outputs are aggregated programmatically. **Sectioning** splits independent subtasks; **voting** repeats the same task.
whyItMatters: Sectioning suits speed or focused attention per aspect; voting suits tasks needing multiple perspectives or attempts for higher-confidence results.
example: Voting: several prompts review the same code for vulnerabilities and flag problems.

definition: A workflow where a central LLM dynamically breaks down a task, delegates subtasks to worker LLMs and synthesizes their results.
whyItMatters: Unlike parallelization, subtasks aren't predefined. It suits complex tasks where you can't predict the subtasks needed, such as multi-file code changes.
example: A coding product that makes complex changes to multiple files each time.

definition: A workflow where one LLM call generates a response while another provides evaluation and feedback, in a loop.
whyItMatters: It fits when there are clear evaluation criteria and iterative refinement provides measurable value.
example: Literary translation, where an evaluator LLM critiques nuances the translator LLM missed.

definition: Anthropic suggests starting with LLM APIs directly, since many patterns take a few lines of code. If you use a framework, understand the underlying code.
whyItMatters: Frameworks can add abstraction that obscures prompts and responses, making debugging harder, and can tempt you to add complexity you do not need.
